title: The Divine Mercy chaplet
hook: on rosary beads: eternal Father, I offer you, and for the sake of his sorrowful passion

segments.voice: Yesterday, devotion: freely chosen, growing around the liturgy and leading back to it. Your line was optional, and loved.

A string of beads with a small crucifix at the end. Anyone would call it a rosary, and it is. But the prayer moving through it today is not the rosary. Someone holding those beads on a bus whispers one short line on each small bead: for the sake of his sorrowful passion, have mercy on us and on the whole world. Same beads, a different prayer. Saint Faustina recorded it in her diary, and it's now prayed far from her convent.
screen: `THE SAME BEADS.` → `A DIFFERENT PRAYER.` → `HAVE MERCY ON US AND ON THE WHOLE WORLD.`

segments.voice: It's built from two movements that take turns. First, an offering. On each large bead, the person praying speaks to God the Father: eternal Father, I offer you. What's offered is Christ himself, his body and blood, soul and divinity, for our sins and those of the whole world. That's a bold thing to say at a kitchen table. It echoes the Mass, where the Church offers Christ to the Father; here, one person with beads joins it in a small way. Second, the asking. On each small bead, the same line: for the sake of his sorrowful passion, have mercy on us and on the whole world. The reason given isn't the person's own goodness. It's Christ's suffering. In Luke, Jesus tells of a man who prays in that spirit. A tax collector stands far back in the Temple, won't lift his eyes, strikes his breast, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner." No list of achievements. Just the request. And it never asks mercy for me alone. It's us, and the whole world: the driver, the stranger across the aisle, the people in the news you can't stand. The chaplet closes by calling God holy, holy and mighty, holy and immortal, and asking once more for mercy. Those titles echo an old hymn of the Eastern churches called the Trisagion, the thrice-holy. So a prayer recorded by a Polish sister ends on words the East has long sung. People pray it alone, in groups, at bedsides, and at three in the afternoon, which is tomorrow's story.
screen: `FIRST, AN OFFERING TO THE FATHER.` · `THEN, THE ASKING.` · `US, AND THE WHOLE WORLD.` · `IT ENDS ON THE THRICE-HOLY.` · then, large: `O GOD, BE MERCIFUL TO ME A SINNER.`

segments.voice: Hold beads if you have them; if not, your fingers will do. If you pray, say the whole chaplet as a prayer card or your parish gives it, or take only the short line, have mercy on us and on the whole world, slowly, a few times. Each time, let a different face come to mind: someone close, someone far away, someone hard to love.
The Divine Mercy chaplet. A short prayer on rosary beads, recorded by Saint Faustina: Christ offered to the Father, and mercy asked for us and the whole world.
Your line: have mercy on us. That us leaves no one out. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Catholics who keep the Divine Mercy devotion pray the chaplet on ordinary rosary beads, alone or in groups, often at three in the afternoon and especially around Divine Mercy Sunday.

chat.says: I saw you praying on rosary beads, but it wasn't the rosary. What was it?
options: The Divine Mercy chaplet. It offers Christ to the Father and asks mercy for us and the whole world.
A shortened rosary. It's the same Hail Marys as the rosary, just said faster on the beads.
A private prayer for myself alone, asking God to forgive only my own sins for the day.
